project.topic: What if Earth hit 1000°F for 5 seconds?
project.title: What if Earth hit 1000°F for 5 seconds?
project.audience: International, curious nontechnical viewers of science shorts (13+).
project.core_question: If the air everywhere hit 1000 °F for five seconds, would you survive, and what would those five seconds actually destroy?
project.viewer_takeaway: Air holds very little heat, so five seconds would burn your skin but probably not kill you. Thin things heat right through: insects die, leaves cook and paper and dry grass ignite, leaving fires and dead foliage behind.

scientific_model.baseline_reality: Near-surface air is about 25 °C (77 °F); people, plants and objects sit near that temperature, and heat moves into them at rates set by convection, radiation and their own thermal mass.
scientific_model.counterfactual_change: For exactly five seconds the air everywhere is 538 °C (1000 °F) at normal pressure, then it returns to normal. The ground, water, people and objects start at their usual temperatures and must absorb heat through their surfaces.
assumptions: Pressure stays normal (no expansion blast); the hot air is dry and still to light breeze.
Exposed skin receives about 11-16 kW/m2: convection (about 6 kW/m2) plus infrared from the hot air column.
Indoors and under water are not shown; the film follows one park.
You wear a sweat-damp cotton tee; a dry synthetic shirt could soften or scorch.
You, the walkers and the fires shown are illustrative.
causal_chain: The air jumps to 538 °C, hotter than the surface of Venus.
Air carries little heat per volume, so in five seconds skin surface reaches about 65-70 °C: a painful burn rather than a lethal one.
Breathing in or open eyes would expose delicate tissue; shutting the eyes and holding the breath avoids the worst.
Thin things heat through: insects pass their thermal limit in about a second, leaves reach boiling point and die; the vapour stays invisible until the air cools.
Thin paper and dead dry grass approach the air temperature, above their autoignition range, so some of it ignites.
When the air cools, the fires keep burning; the cooked foliage browns and annual crops are damaged.
uncertainties: Heat flux to skin depends strongly on wind and the hot air’s infrared emission; burns could range from first to second degree.
Paper and dry grass ignition timing depends on thickness and moisture.
Whether trees regrow leaves and how much of a harvest is lost depend on species and season.
Deaths among vulnerable people, birds and animals are not estimated here.
Water vapour boiled off the leaves is invisible in 538 °C air; it shows as steam only after the air cools.
"Most of the world’s leaves" excludes plants under snow or water and thick succulent leaves.

claims.statement: The scenario sets the air to 538 °C (1000 °F) for five seconds at normal pressure.
claims.presentation_guardrail: Say "a thousand degrees" with the °F HUD; do not imply the ground or water become that hot.

claims.statement: That is hotter than the surface of Venus, about 870-900 °F (465-480 °C).
claims.reasoning: NASA gives Venus’s average surface temperature as about 870 °F and quotes up to 900 °F.
claims.presentation_guardrail: Compare temperature only; Venus also has 90x the pressure.

claims.statement: Air holds very little heat, so in five seconds only the outer skin of a person heats up and brief exposure to very hot dry air is survivable.
claims.reasoning: At room temperature air holds about 1/3500 as much heat per volume as water, and at 538 °C it is 2.7x less dense (about 1/9000); Blagden’s 1775 experiments showed people enduring dry air above 100 °C for minutes.
claims.presentation_guardrail: The pizza-oven comparison describes the feeling (an oven dome radiates a similar ~15 kW/m2), not safety.

claims.statement: Five seconds at about 11-16 kW/m2 gives exposed skin a painful first-degree burn and possibly some blistering, but is unlikely to be lethal for a healthy adult who shuts their eyes and does not inhale.
claims.reasoning: Thermal dose (q^4/3 t) of about 120-200 units sits between the first-degree (~105) and second-degree (~290) thresholds; NOAA burn tables give severe pain in ~5 s and second-degree burns in ~14 s at 10 kW/m2.
claims.presentation_guardrail: Say "probably survive"; children, the elderly and people who inhale fare worse.

claims.statement: Shutting the eyes and not breathing in protects the most delicate tissues for a few seconds.
claims.reasoning: Eyelids and closed airways keep hot air off the cornea and airway lining; inhaled dry hot air mostly injures the upper airway.
claims.presentation_guardrail: Advice for this fictional scenario only.

claims.statement: Leaves heat to boiling point within about a second and are killed, browning over the next day; leaf tissue typically dies above about 50 °C.
claims.reasoning: A leaf (~0.6 kJ/m2K, both faces exposed) approaches the air temperature until its water boils; global surveys put leaf thermal limits near 41-54 °C.
claims.presentation_guardrail: Cooked leaves brown over the next day; many trees can regrow from buds.

claims.statement: Flying insects heat through and pass their thermal limit (about 40-50 °C) in about a second.
claims.reasoning: Tiny bodies have time constants well under a second; measured insect critical thermal maxima are typically 40-50 °C.
claims.presentation_guardrail: Insects in soil, hives or water are not covered.

claims.statement: Thin paper and dead dry grass approach the air temperature within seconds, above paper’s 218-246 °C autoignition range, so some of it ignites within the five seconds.
claims.reasoning: Newspaper (~0.06 kJ/m2K) has a heating time constant of about a second at these heat-transfer rates; dry fine fuels behave similarly. Autoignition figures come from minute-long tests, so ignition within five seconds is likely but not certain.
claims.presentation_guardrail: Green, wet plants steam rather than burn.

claims.statement: Fires started during the five seconds keep burning after the air cools, so many fires would start at once.
claims.reasoning: Once ignited, flaming combustion sustains itself in normal air.

claims.statement: Annual crops whose leaves are cooked wilt, damaging this season’s harvest.
claims.reasoning: Leaf death removes photosynthesis; recovery depends on growth stage and species.

creative_direction.logline: The air hits a thousand degrees for five seconds: you walk away burned, but everything thinner than you cooks or catches fire.
creative_direction.visual_identity: A bright summer park slowed to bullet time under an orange heat grade and shimmer; small things fail in the background, then the colour snaps back to a world of smoke and brown leaves.
creative_direction.lighting: Hard summer sun with blue-sky fill (sun-skylight-rig-v1); flames add warm flicker; next day a hazy, smoky sun.
creative_direction.camera_language: Eye-level handheld POV and tracking shots at 1.4-1.6 m around a slowed jogger; low close-ups in the flower bed and under a canopy; a wide look up at the smoke over the skyline.
creative_direction.motion_language: Speed ramp at the hit: the world runs 7.3x slow for five event-seconds, then snaps back; insects fold and fall, leaves darken, paper and litter ignite at their own times.
creative_direction.world_scale_policy: Metre scale throughout; insects slightly enlarged for legibility; the farm is a second location 1.5 km east.
creative_direction.opening_hook: Out jogging, the air hits a thousand degrees Fahrenheit. Your face stings.
creative_direction.mid_video_rehook: The danger flips: you survive because you are thick, but anything thinner than you heats all the way through, so leaves cook, insects drop and paper ignites.
creative_direction.ending_payoff: Five seconds is too short to cook a person and long enough to cook the leaves outdoors.
creative_direction.loop_connection: The final frame returns to the same park and path where the jog began, now brown.
creative_direction.asset_policy: Reuse grass, tree, flame, smoke, Humanoid and sun rig; story-local bench, newspaper, insects and skyline; add an optional heatHaze setting to film-pipeline-v1.

audio.voice_style: Crisp, urgent, fascinated adult male; high-tension simulation narrator; brisk opening cadence
audio.music_direction: Original score: light morning groove cut off by a deep heat roar, slowed heartbeat and stretched drones through the five seconds, crackle and hiss textures, a silence as the heat ends, then sparse sober chords for the aftermath.
audio.sfx_direction: 0.3 s silence before the hit and before the end; heat whoomp; slowed footsteps and heartbeat; steam hiss; paper and grass ignition whumps aligned to their frames; crackling fires; distant sirens.

distribution.primary_search_intent: what if earth hit 1000 degrees for 5 seconds, could you survive 1000 degrees, hotter than venus
distribution.distinctive_angle: The heat that sounds lethal mostly spares you because air holds so little energy; the real damage falls on everything thinner than you.
distribution.comment_bait_question: Where would you want to be for those five seconds?
distribution.seo_integrity_note: Fictional five-second pulse of 1000 °F air at normal pressure; burn, leaf and ignition outcomes are estimates; the people and fires shown are illustrative.
